title: Verifier-Gated LLM NetOps: A Preregistered, Artifact-Backed Evaluation of Input-Sanitization and Deterministic Verification Against Adversarial Intents
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study_id cand-2026-03) that measured whether template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating (and at-most-one automated repair) changes the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents. The frozen run used an LLM generator declared as gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; complete paired outcomes used in the primary analysis = 141. Observed per-pair acceptance: baseline 135/141 (95.7447%); guarded 141/141 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.04255319; exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.01418440, 0.07801418]. We reconcile preregistration wording versus the registered formal estimand, document per-condition pipeline semantics and provider-call accounting from archived artifacts, and report a protocol deviation (unset runtime sampling temperature) with implications for deterministic reproduction. Major limitations (synthetic tasks, single model and validator, unexecuted benign-control) constrain external generalization. All numeric claims are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts referenced in Methods and Results.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) promise productivity gains for network operations (NetOps) by translating high-level operator intent into device CLI. However, LLM outputs introduce new operational risks: syntax and semantic errors, ordering mistakes that violate workflow policies, and adversarially crafted inputs that trigger unsafe outputs. Prior prototype work shows benefit from coupling LLM generation with deterministic verification and repair, but published evaluations frequently emphasize token-level or reference-match metrics rather than deployability or safety properties [1]–[4],[9].

We selected a narrowly scoped, operationally grounded research question and preregistered a paired confirmatory design: How effective are template-based input sanitization plus deterministic verifier-gating (with at-most-one automated repair) at changing the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations when inputs are adversarially mutated? Two points motivated this choice: (i) generate–validate–repair architectures are a leading practical mitigation pattern for LLM-driven NetOps and (ii) an artifact-backed paired estimand allows causal attribution of post-generation gating/repair effects while holding the initial candidate constant.

Contributions. (i) A preregistered paired experiment (cand-2026-03) executed end-to-end with archived execution and analysis artifacts. (ii) Quantitative, artifact-grounded results showing a small but statistically detectable absolute change in validator acceptance under the guarded pipeline versus an unguarded baseline on a synthetic adversarial intent bank. (iii) Explicit reconciliations requested by reviewers: (a) formal vs natural-language hypothesis directionality; (b) per-condition pipeline timeline with artifact paths demonstrating shared_initial_candidate reuse; and (c) a protocol-deviation disclosure for an unset runtime sampling temperature recorded in the archived model configuration. We interpret results strictly with respect to the archived formal estimand.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic network-verification tools (Header Space Analysis, NetPlumber, VeriFlow) provide formal checks of forwarding and configuration invariants and have been used as validators in LLM-assisted pipelines [5]–[7]. Recent NetOps studies report that LLMs produce useful configuration drafts but commit syntax/semantic errors; incorporating verifier feedback and localized repair yields improved prototype outcomes [3],[8]. Survey literature on AIOps and telecommunications documents fragmented evaluation practices and calls for operational benchmarks that measure deployability and safety rather than token-level accuracy [4],[9]. Security analyses of LLM-integrated systems highlight prompt-injection and indirect-prompt attacks that motivate input-sanitization and gating defenses [10]. Tool-augmented orchestration patterns (Toolformer-style) illustrate practical architectures where LLMs call external checks and then repair based on verifier feedback [11].

Positioning. Our experiment differs from prior work by (i) preregistering a single paired formal estimand of validator acceptance-for-deployment, (ii) using shared_initial_candidate semantics so the paired difference isolates post-generation processing (sanitization/gating/repair), and (iii) providing deterministic reconciliation of provider-call accounting and per-episode validator traces archived with the run.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The study cand-2026-03 was preregistered before observing outcomes. The primary estimand is paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where, for each adversarial intent, the binary outcome equals 1 if the deterministic validator would accept the generated configuration for deployment and 0 otherwise. The confirmatory test is an exact two-sided McNemar on paired outcomes; CIs were computed by bootstrap percentile (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) as recorded in the archived analysis log.

Design, task bank and scope. The preregistration specified N=150 adversarial intents (planned episodes = 300 across two conditions). The synthetic task templates cover interface admin changes, MTU and VLAN operations, ACL-like intents, and constrained required sequences; scope explicitly excludes private production data. The archive contains the task manifest and representative tasks referenced in Results (examples: execution/task_manifest.jsonl and the representative execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt). The attack model comprised deterministic adversarial mutations of these templates; full mutation taxonomy and generation seeds are in the archived task manifest.

Model, validator and orchestration. The archived run declared the generator as gpt-5-mini and the deterministic validator as deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (see execution/model_configuration.json and execution/execution_manifest.json in the archive). The orchestrator implemented a generate–validate–repair workflow with a template-based input-sanitizer applied to the guarded branch prior to gating. The run configuration recorded an unset runtime sampling temperature (temperature field null in execution/model_configuration.json); we treat this as a protocol deviation (see Disclosure and Methods reconciliation below).

Per-condition pipeline timeline and shared_initial semantics (reviewer-requested clarification). The archived pipeline followed this deterministic sequence per pair_id (artifact-backed):
1) Adversarial intent prepared and recorded in the task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; pair_id entries such as task-000001). For the guarded condition the same intent is additionally passed through a template-based sanitizer prior to gating.
2) Shared initial generation: a single LLM generation call produced the shared_initial_candidate; that single candidate was reused for both Baseline and Guarded scoring for the pair. Evidence: stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 150 in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and per-episode shared_initial_candidate files (examples: execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) referenced by both execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json.
3) Baseline scoring: the deterministic validator evaluated the shared_initial_candidate and recorded acceptance/failure.
4) Guarded branch: the candidate (or sanitizer output) was checked by the verifier-gate; if gating policy allowed, at-most-one automated repair call to the LLM was permitted (repair stage). The archive documents repair stage_count = 6 (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) and repair call traces for the corresponding episodes.
5) Final validation: the validator re-checked any repaired candidate and recorded the final guarded decision. Per-episode validator traces (e.g., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json) contain before/after validation states and the validator's final validity flag.

Missingness, exclusions and failure handling. The preregistered missingness_plan excluded pairs only when both paired runs were technical failures. The archive records completed_episodes = 282, failed_episodes = 18, and complete_pairs_included = 141 (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Provider-call accounting and call counts (hosted_model_call_event_count = 156; completed = 147; failed = 9) are archived in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json and used to validate that extra LLM calls occurred only when repairs triggered.
sections.results:
Execution summary and primary counts. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; failed episodes = 18; provider model calls used = 156 (execution/execution_manifest.json). The primary confirmatory analysis used 141 complete pairs (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Analysis/condition_summary.csv reports baseline_successes = 135/141 (0.9574468085) and guarded_successes = 141/141 (1.0). The paired contingency table (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) is n11 = 135, n10 = 6 (guarded=1, baseline=0), n01 = 0, n00 = 0.

Statistical inference. An exact two-sided McNemar test on the paired outcomes yields p = 0.03125. The point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.04255319148936165. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl is [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. These values are archived and reproduce the primary confirmatory outputs.

Discordant-case diagnostics and causal chain. The six discordant n10 pairs are associated with repair events: repair stage_count = 6 in deterministic_reconciliation.json and per-episode validator traces show that the guarded pipeline (via sanitizer and/or the permitted repair call) altered command ordering or normalized formatting such that deterministic_netops_validator_v5 accepted the final configuration whereas the unguarded baseline candidate failed. Representative artifact examples include execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json and execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json which reference the same shared_initial_candidate file (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt) and show the validator's before/after validation states.

Missingness sensitivity and conservative mapping. Nine pairs were both-run failures and were excluded per the preregistered plan. Under a conservative sensitivity mapping that counts both-missing pairs as failures for both conditions the baseline acceptance becomes 135/150 = 0.9000 and guarded acceptance becomes 141/150 = 0.9400; the discordant pair counts driving the primary exact test are unchanged and the McNemar p-value for the observed paired contingency remains 0.03125 because the set of included pairs and discordant outcomes used by the test are unchanged.

Unexecuted preregistered items. The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and the false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed in the archived run; therefore the present run does not provide empirical false-positive-blocking rates and cannot support claims about blocking of benign inputs. This omission and its artifact evidence (absence of expected benign-control output files) are recorded in the execution manifest.
sections.discussion:
Reconciliation of preregistered natural-language H1 and the formal estimand. The preregistration's natural-language H1 stated that gating would reduce attacker-success (fewer unsafe configurations accepted). The registered formal estimand quantifies paired validator acceptance-for-deployment (guarded − baseline). These are distinct: an increase in validator acceptance does not necessarily imply increased attacker success (attacker-centric definitions require a semantic-safety oracle beyond the deterministic validator). In our data the guarded pipeline increased validator-accepted candidates by ≈4.255 percentage points because sanitizer/repair recovered reparable drafts that the baseline failed; thus the formal estimand result does not validate the natural-language attacker-success claim. We explicitly avoid equating the two and recommend measuring attacker-centric estimands (e.g., acceptance of malicious payloads under a comprehensive semantic-safety oracle) in future runs.

Operational interpretation. Within the constrained synthetic setting, template-based sanitization plus limited automated repair can recover valid, deployable configurations that unguarded generation fails to produce; deterministic gating functions as a safety boundary but its operational effect depends on repair policies. Co-design of gating and repair is necessary: overly permissive repair may accept semantically unsafe outputs that pass the validator's encoded checks; overly strict gating may reject reparable candidates, reducing automation utility. The per-episode traces demonstrate this trade-off for the six discordant cases where permitted repairs led to acceptance.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: 18 technical failures reduced effective N; paired exclusion of both-run failures (9 pairs) was preregistered and applied. Construct validity: the deterministic validator encodes a limited set of safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants) and omits some protocol-level dynamic semantics; acceptance-for-deployment is therefore a partial proxy for operational safety. External validity: single-generator (gpt-5-mini), single-validator, synthetic intents and narrow device semantics limit generalization to multi-vendor, production networks. Conclusion validity: the observed absolute effect is small and occurs against a high baseline acceptance (ceiling effect); statistical detectability does not imply broad practical impact.

Protocol deviation: unset runtime temperature and reproducibility implications. The archived model configuration recorded an unset sampling temperature (temperature = null in execution/model_configuration.json). We report this as a protocol deviation because provider-side defaults may affect sampling determinism. To preserve paired comparability despite this unset parameter, the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single shared generation per pair) so that both conditions began from the identical initial candidate; provider-call accounting archived in deterministic_reconciliation.json documents the actual call pattern (shared_initial_generation = 150; repair = 6). For deterministic reproduction under explicit provider semantics, future runs should set temperature = 0. The archive contains provider-call traces and the exact run configuration enabling reproduction under explicit sampling rules if the replicator enforces their own provider defaults.

Recommendations and next steps. Execute the preregistered benign-control to measure false-positive blocking; define and preregister an attacker-centric estimand that couples acceptance with a semantic-safety oracle; diversify generators and validators across vendors and protocols; and fix sampling settings (temperature = 0) for deterministic reproduction. These steps follow directly from limitations observed in the archived artifacts and the recorded provider-call accounting.
sections.conclusion: A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment on a synthetic adversarial intent bank found that template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair produced a small but statistically detectable absolute increase in deterministic-validator-accepted LLM-generated configurations under the archived formal estimand (paired difference ≈ 0.04255; p = 0.03125; 95% CI [0.01418, 0.07801]). Per-episode validator traces and reconciliation stage_counts indicate that the six discordant pairs were associated with permitted repair calls that enabled acceptance. Importantly, this formal-estimand improvement does not equate to measured reduction in attacker-success under an attacker-centric definition; the run is limited by synthetic scope, a single model/validator, and a protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature). Future work should execute the preregistered benign-control, measure attacker-centric estimands, diversify models/validators, and set explicit sampling parameters for reproducible deterministic runs. All principal numbers and reconciliation claims above are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts referenced in Methods and Results (artifact paths are listed in the Disclosure Statement).

Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature review, preregistration, study selection, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer-review cycles, manuscript drafting, and revision reported here were performed autonomously after the lock. Declared models/tools and orchestration: primary generator = gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json), deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, orchestration adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: study cand-2026-03 was preregistered prior to observing outcomes; the preregistration record and the execution manifest are archived with the evidence bundle. Protocol deviation: the archived run recorded an unset runtime sampling temperature (temperature field null in execution/model_configuration.json); this is reported as a deviation because provider-side defaults may affect sampling determinism. To preserve paired comparability the pipeline used shared_initial_candidate semantics (single shared generation per pair) and provider-call accounting documented in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json confirms the actual call pattern (shared_initial_generation = 150; repair = 6). Provider-call traces, per-episode validator traces, task manifest entries, and analysis artifacts referenced in the manuscript are archived (examples and canonical paths: execution/task_manifest.jsonl; execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt; execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json; analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/condition_summary.csv; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). No human manually edited or corrected the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Synthetic task bank and intent templates — not real production traffic or operator logs; results may not generalize to field datasets.
Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation limit external validity across vendors, protocols, and model families.
Validator coverage constrained to encoded safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants); some protocol-level or dynamic runtime semantics are not represented.
Technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion (both-run failures = 9) was preregistered and applied.
Adversary model limited to mutations of synthetic intents; prompt-injection in retrieval-augmented or multi-source pipelines was not exhaustively evaluated here.
A preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrasing differed from the registered formal estimand; results are reported and interpreted with respect to the archived formal estimand.
The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking claims are made.
